transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-05 15:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Location: Video call (recorded)

Attendees:
- Jordan Ellis (Redwood, AE)
- Priya Menon (Redwood, SE)
- Marta Lopez (Avalanche, Head of Data)
- Ethan Wu (Avalanche, Platform Eng)
- Ravi Patel (Avalanche, VP Product)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, noisy):
Avalanche is evaluating per-message cost for a customer-facing chat product, trying to decide between Redwood hosted API vs reserved dedicated pools vs private V P C deployment. Key constraints: < $0.002 per convo target for baseline flows, P95 latency under 220ms for short prompts, and strict data residency for EU customers. They asked about batching, KV cache, quantization tradeoffs, and pilot timelines.

Topics covered:
- Current cost model and traffic shape
- Tokenization and average token per message
- Batching and batch size controls + latency impact
- KV / prefix caching for chat sessions
- Dedicated vs hosted pricing bands and SLAs
- Pilot scope and success criteria

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. Quick intros, then we dig into the per-message econ questions Marta flagged.
[00:12] Marta: Hi, Marta here. Thanks. We're trying to understand the unit economics — per message, per conversation — for our multi-tenant chat assistant.
[00:19] Ethan: Hey all, Ethan, I run platform infra. We'll likely start with hosted to move fast but want to know how that scales cost-wise and when dedicated/private makes sense.
[00:27] Jordan: Cool — Priya's our SE, she'll cover the microbenchmarks and latency/batching stuff. Priya, take it away.
[00:33] Priya (SE): Thanks. First high-level — Redwood supports hosted API, Dedicated reserved GPU pools, and Private VPC installs. For per-message cost the levers are token price, batching, and caching. Also quantization and model choice.
[00:47] Ravi: Quick clarification — when you say token price, is that per input token, output token, both? We mostly care about total tokens per convo.
[00:55] Priya: Right — our hosted pricing is per input + output tokens, embeddings are per-vector. For Dedicated we do committed capacity pricing — lower unit cost once you commit, but you pay for reserved GPUs. Private has a different licensing model.
[01:10] Marta: Our goal is roughly $0.0015 - $0.002 per typical short conversation. Typical convo length is around 180-220 tokens total, often 1-2 short back-and-forths. Peak concurrency ~250 users, baseline 40 rps.
[01:28] Jordan: Ok, nice baseline. So for hosted, rough calc — if hosted base rate is X per 1k tokens, that maps to Y per convo; batching can bring per-token servo down if you can batch multiple requests.
[01:40] Ethan: How does continuous batching affect tail latency? We can't have big spikes for interactive users.
[01:47] Priya: Continuous batching optimizes throughput by grouping similar length requests. We have latency SLO tiers; for interactive flows we advise small batch sizes or latency-first routing which reduces batch size and keeps P95 low. There's an operational knob — target latency vs cost.
[02:03] Marta: What's KV cache? Is that the convo history caching?
[02:07] Priya: Yes — KV cache (sometimes mis-transcribed as K V cash) stores transformer key-value tensors client-side on the GPU runtime between requests to avoid recomputing the prefix, which saves tokens for certain usage patterns. For chat, if you have many short back-and-forths, prefix caching can cut compute ~30-60% depending on history length.
[02:26] Ravi: So caching reduces compute but doesn't change token billing right?
[02:30] Priya: Correct — token billing is based on tokens sent/returned; caching reduces GPU cycles and therefore unit cost on Dedicated/Private, and for Hosted it reduces billed compute portion in our model, though token billing still applies. There's nuance: if you avoid resending history tokens by storing state server-side and only send deltas, you can reduce token counts.
[02:47] Ethan: Hmm, so we could implement delta sends to minimize token counts; we are worried about data residency if we store session state outside EU.
[02:55] Jordan: That ties into hosted vs private decisions. Hosted can be region-limited to EU regions, but Private/VPC gives you full control over where state lives.
[03:04] Marta: On numbers — Priya, can you walk us through a worked example for 200-token convo with and without batching/caching?
[03:11] Priya: Sure. Hypothetical: model A hosted rate 0.04 USD per 1k tokens input+output. So 200 tokens -> 0.008 per convo before batching. If you batch many short requests, effective compute amortization lowers our internal compute-based portion — say a 30% reduction → ~0.0056 per convo. With KV caching and delta sends removing 60 tokens of history from each request, tokens drop to 140 → base is 0.0056 → with batching + caching maybe ~0.0039. But on Dedicated, unit compute cost is lower, so similar workload might be 0.0025 per convo after batching and cache. These are approximate.
[03:51] Ravi: That helps. So our $0.002 target seems reachable with Dedicated or Private if we commit and optimize token deltas and caching.
[03:58] Jordan: Right. Also model choice matters; 7B quantized models often reduce costs at a slight quality drop. We recommend running evals against your prompts.
[04:07] Marta: Any gotchas on quantization? We have some regulated flows with PHI-like data, though not full healthcare.
[04:13] Priya: Quantization is supported in Dedicated and Private; hosted supports certain quantized variants too. For regulated data, encryption at rest and KMS integrations are available for Private; for Hosted we provide audit logs and SOC2 but if you need full control over keys, Private is the path.
[04:28] Ethan: On SLA side — if we go Dedicated, what's the latency guarantee? We need P95 under 220ms for under 256 token requests.
[04:36] Priya: We have SLA tiers tied to capacity commitments; Dedicated pools can be provisioned and we can commit to P95 targets for the specified workload curve. We'll ask to run a pilot with your workload shape to validate.
[04:48] Jordan: Regarding pilot — typical approach: 2-week pilot on hosted with synthetic-matched traffic + 3 day dedicated microbench if you want to validate the reserved approach. Priya can run the microbench.
[05:00] Marta: Timeline question — we want a decision in two weeks. Can we get pricing and the benchmarks in that window?
[05:05] Jordan: Yes — I'll send pilot pricing worksheet within 48 hours and Priya will run the microbench and upload results within 5 business days.
[05:12] Ravi: About billing granularity: do you expose per-route token breakdown? We need to know cost per feature to attribute to product lines.
[05:20] Priya: Redwood Console exposes token-level breakdown per route and model, token bucket usage, per-request latency, and trace IDs to map to your logs. You can export CSVs for finance.
[05:29] Ethan: Any hidden costs? Networking, egress?
[05:33] Jordan: For Hosted we include API egress in price generally, but large embedding outputs or bulk downloads can incur network charges in some scenarios — we'll call that out in the worksheet. Dedicated has infrastructure charges bundled in the reserved price; Private will have a license + your infra costs. We'll itemize.
[05:47] Marta: Competitors — we evaluated OpenAI and Anthropic earlier. We're leaning away from full self-host because of ops overhead, but we might go Private later.
[05:56] Priya: Totally reasonable. Many customers start hosted to validate UX then move to Dedicated when they need predictable unit economics and to Private for residency/regulatory constraints.
[06:06] Ethan: About batching controls — can we set per-route batch size and latency target? E.g., payments flow gets latency-first, analytics flow can be cost-first.
[06:15] Priya: Yes — routing policies by route, model, or token-size; you can set latency SLOs and Redwood will route to lower-latency capacity or fall back to cheaper model variants if SLO allows.
[06:25] Ravi: Do you support automatic fallback to smaller models when load increases?
[06:28] Priya: Yep — smart routing + fallback policies. You can configure a cascade: primary high-quality model, fallback mid-sized quantized, then a basic cheap model. Logs show fallbacks so you can detect regressions.
[06:39] Marta: For our security/compliance folks — do you have SOC 2 Type II? ISO?
[06:44] Jordan: We have SOC 2 Type II; ISO in progress for certain regions. For Private we support KMS/HSM integrations and audit logs. I'll share the security pack.
[06:53] Ethan: One more technical — how much savings from K V cache realistically on dialogue heavy workloads?
[06:58] Priya: Depends a lot. If your average history is 8 turns, caching avoids re-encoding/attention on the prefix; customers report 25–55% compute saving on interactive chat flows. But token billing only drops if you stop sending history. So pairing server-side session storage + delta sends is best.
[07:16] Ravi: Are there privacy tradeoffs storing session state server-side? GDPR implications?
[07:20] Priya: Yes you need to ensure residency and data subject rights; Private host gives full control, Hosted can be region-locked but has data processing agreements. We can share our DPA.
[07:30] Marta: Great. Can you put together two scenarios — conservative and aggressive — with numbers for hosted vs dedicated vs private so we can present to finance?
[07:38] Jordan: Absolutely. We'll produce a short spreadsheet: baseline token assumptions, batch/caching deltas, unit costs per model, and expected cost per convo under three configurations.
[07:47] Ethan: For the microbench — Priya, what inputs do you need? We'll provide representative prompts and sample concurrency curves.
[07:53] Priya: We'll need: sample prompt set, token counts, target concurrency curve (p50/p95), and whether you want latency-first or cost-first routing for each route. Also your compliance/region list to pick regions.
[08:05] Marta: We'll send that by EOD tomorrow.
[08:08] Jordan: Perfect. Last note — if you want to trial Dedicated we'd build a 30-day reserved pool trial with limited commit to prove unit econ before signing a longer term contract.
[08:18] Ravi: Sounds good. Any other questions?
[08:21] Ethan: One small ask — can Redwood provide an example of model degradation/regression detection? We want to ensure fallback doesn't silently reduce quality.
[08:29] Priya: Yes — Redwood Optimize gives prompt-set evals and regression alerts; we can tie alerts to rollbacks. We'll demo that in the next session if you like.
[08:37] Marta: That would be helpful.
[08:40] Jordan: Ok summary of next steps: I share pilot pricing worksheet, Priya uploads microbenchmarks, Avalanche sends prompts and concurrency shape, and Marta confirms compliance list. We'll reconvene once benchmark results are in.
[08:52] Ravi: Thanks all.
[08:55] Jordan: Thanks everyone — end call.
